newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO set up committee on Hebron.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO set up committee on Hebron.

text.p: Israel and the PLO on Sunday held their first talks since a wave of violence put their peace deals in danger.

They agreed during almost three hours of U.S.-mediated talks at the Israel-Gaza border to set a committee to work on implementing a long-delayed Israeli troop redeployment from the West Bank city of Hebron.
"The parties reiterated their commitment to Oslo and its implementation," said Israeli negotiator Dore Gold, referring to Israel-PLO peace deals forged in the Norwegian capital.

"We have a difficult task ahead of us. We are determined to exert every possible effort to expedite the implementation of the interim (peace) agreement on the ground," chief Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat told reporters after the talks.

Erekat and chief Israeli negotiator Dan Shomron said Israel and the PLO would activate a committee on Hebron redeployment but had yet to agree on a venue. Israel Television said the Hebron committee would meet on Monday at the Gaza-Israel border.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher, dispatched to the region after an emergency PLO-Israeli summit at the White House last week, said the situation between Israel and the PLO was still dangerous although tensions had eased.
Christopher said Israel's new right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu assured him on Sunday he would carry out signed agreements with the PLO.
Christopher said he hoped his meeting with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat would help move the peace process forward.
"The recent violence has demonstrated the great urgency of reaching some concrete results just as soon as possible," Christopher told a news conference with Netanyahu in Jerusalem.
After meeting Arafat in the PLO-ruled Gaza Strip Christopher said: "The situation has eased somewhat...but it is still a dangerous situation."
Christopher did not take part in the Erez talks between the teams of lower-level negotiators including U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross.

Resumption of these talks was the main achievement of President Bill Clinton's hastily convened summit last week to save five years of U.S.-mediated peace negotiations threatened by violence that killed 58 Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers.

Netanyahu, whose opening of a tunnel near Jerusalem's Moslem holy places triggered that violence, said Israel sought a joint recommitment with the Palestinians to their peace accords. But he declined to set a date for a troop redeployment from Hebron, delayed since March.
Netanyahu sought to calm Palestinian fears that he wanted to rewrite the Oslo agreement signed by his Labour party predecessors.
"We suggested that within the confines of the existing agreement adjustments be made," he told the news conference.
Netanyahu wants to modify security arrangements for Jewish settlers in Hebron, the last of seven West Bank towns to be given self-rule.
In Gaza Christopher picked up this point.
"One of the things that has been clarified during my visit here is that the parties intend to negotiate within the four corners of the agreement," he said. "They do not seek to modify."
Asked if he was reassured by this, Arafat said: "We'll wait and see."
Arafat has sought international support for his stance. Clinton, four weeks before a presidential election, has been loathe to lean on Netanyahu, but the European Union has sought to play a role.
Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring arrived in Israel on Sunday and met Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy.
Christopher seemed cool to direct European involvement, saying "any major change in the bilateral character of these negotiations is not likely to take place".
